text: A shared-LUN clustered filesystem written entirely by AI. Every line of the clustering, coordination, distributed-lock, fencing, and on-disk-envelope code in this repository was written by AI — not by a human using an AI tool. Claude Opus, running as an autonomous coding agent in Anthropic's Claude Code, wrote a large share of it, consulting Claude Fable, GPT, Gemini and Astra on the hardest problems. MeshXFS starts from the upstream Linux kernel XFS code, written by the XFS developers, and the AI has since modified much of it heavily (see "How this was built"). Everything that turns XFS into a filesystem many machines can mount at once is AI-authored. 0.90.130: Stronger Recovery, Broader Platform Support What changed for someone upgrading from 0.90.129: The network lock manager over multipath, at 2, 4, 8 and 16 nodes, and over a single path at 8 and 16 (0.90.130). A node that loses every storage path is fenced and its journal replayed while the others keep writing; every other node now refuses the fenced node's late lock releases before recovery collects its locks, so none of them can land afterwards and leave the filesystem refusing every write. Ubuntu 26.04 and Debian 12 are supported (0.90.130): the .deb, on Ubuntu 26.04's kernel 7.0 and Debian 12's 6.1. Fixes (0.90.130): on kernels before 6.5 (Debian 12) every buffered write now advances the file position (it rewrote the same offset); a node frozen by a backup or snapshot tool ( fsfreeze ) answers another node's lock request without a kernel warning, which on a host that sets panic_on_warn was a crash; on kernels before 6.6 a userspace thaw no longer ends the freeze a node holds while another node joins. "Installed packages" means the release packages on two nodes of each supported platform: Proxmox VE 9 (kernels 6.17 and 7.0), RHEL 9.8, Ubuntu 24.04, Ubuntu 26.04, Debian 12 and Debian 13. Every host in a cluster needs the same MeshXFS version; hosts on different kernels are fine. 0.90.129: Shared Proxmox Storage, Faster DRBD Setup, Stronger Recovery What changed for someone upgrading from 0.90.124, the last published release (0.90.125 to 0.90.128 were never published; their work ships here): Proxmox VE 9 hosts share one SAN LUN as their datastore, over multipath (0.90.129). Three hosts on one iSCSI LUN over two storage networks run guests on it: live migration with the guest writing throughout, HA restart after a host loses power, snapshots and rollback, backup and restore, disk moves, templates and linked clones, containers, and a storage path lost and returned under load. Verified on both Proxmox VE 9 kernels: 6.17, which the 9.1 installer ships, and 7.0, which proxmox-default-kernel now installs. A DRBD pair is set up in minutes, on whole disks (0.90.129). The guide gives DRBD the disk that will hold the VMs and skips DRBD's first copy of it, which took about an hour per 250 GB: the device is formatted next, so nothing on it before is ever read. Two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts set up this way wrote at the replication link's full speed and passed live migration, datastore operations, a full disk, a host reset under load, a host leaving and returning cleanly, and the 31-row suite, on both kernels, and through a rolling kernel upgrade with one host on each. A DRBD pair whose first host dies recovers, given a QDevice (0.90.128): authority=quorum in /etc/mxfs/drbd-fence.conf lets corosync's vote decide which host carries on. Fixes to locking and recovery (0.90.128, 0.90.129): a host that dies no longer stalls the others for a minute; a new lock tenure is no longer taken for one already released; a waiter registration that fails no longer leaves its mark on the lock; a fenced host reports being fenced, not corruption; a new file on a reused inode number no longer crashes its creator; a shared mmap write no longer hangs on RHEL 9; a full DRBD filesystem refuses a write at once instead of hanging the writer. vSphere shared disks (0.90.128): MeshXFS mounts a multi-writer VMDK or a physical-mode RDM with fence=vcenter , fence=manual or fence=quorum . Not yet a released configuration. The module's messages say MeshXFS (0.90.128), not XFS, and the product is named MeshXFS throughout (0.90.125). Proxmox VM disk settings are documented (0.90.129): give VM disks on MeshXFS cache=none , the Proxmox default and the mode every Proxmox validation ran with (see "Proxmox VE: VM disk settings" below). "Installed packages" means the release packages on two nodes of each released platform: Proxmox VE 9 (kernels 6.17 and 7.0), RHEL 9.8, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13. Every host in a cluster needs the same MeshXFS version; hosts on different kernels are fine. 0.90.124: Multipath SAN Support, Stronger Recovery, Better Scalability What changed for someone upgrading from 0.90.116, the last published release: dm-multipath is released again for SAN clusters on the on-disk lock manager (0.90.124): 2/disk/caw/mpath , 4/disk/caw/mpath , 8/disk/caw/mpath and 16/disk/caw/mpath . Every node reaches the shared iSCSI LUN through a dm-multipath map over two paths, each on its own NIC and storage network. It was last claimed in 0.90.51, and later releases dropped it when defects found since then reached it. Fixed on the way there (0.90.123, 0.90.124), each found by the 16-node path-fault runs: a node acquiring a directory could wait on a child's lock that a peer held while that peer waited for the same directory, stalling every node for eight minutes; a node that rejoined after being fenced could fail to open a file, its open() retrying for ever and impossible to kill; and an open that can never be granted now fails with EIO, while a killed open always returns. More than one MeshXFS filesystem can be mounted on a host (0.90.120). Before, two filesystems on the same hosts crossed each other's lock traffic: connections were reset, one filesystem could miss its peer's heartbeat, and fsyncs took 17 s instead of 0.6 s. A new mount option, transport=tcp|caw , picks each filesystem's lock manager, so one host can keep a DRBD resource mounted beside a SAN LUN. A DRBD pair with several MeshXFS resources recovers every one of them (0.90.121, 0.90.122). When a host died, only one resource recovered and the others stayed blocked; now each is fenced and recovered under its own evidence. When one replication link fails, the peer is cut off on every resource the two hosts share, where before a mount could shut down or hang. The module is now loaded before DRBD connects, because loading it with links up could drop them. Less wasted lock work under heavy VM load on a DRBD pair (0.90.117, 0.90.118). With seven AlmaLinux installs at once on two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts with 2011-era SATA SSDs, the lock answers a host wrote for requests the other host had already abandoned fell from 84 to 17, and the longest a request waited in the answering host's queue fell from 39 s to 13 s. An allocation now stops asking a host that has stopped answering: the longest allocation walk fell from 46 s to 8.5 s. A misleading kernel warning is gone (0.90.117): P958-ACQ-IDLE-LOST read like a lock wait of up to 20 minutes, but every one was the leftover record of a brief try that had already given up. Still open: under heavy load on slow disks, a VM write that needs new space can still wait about a second for a slow answer from the other host of a DRBD pair (D-REMOTE-NOQUEUE-AG-TRYLOCK-WAITS-A-FULL-ATTEMPT-PER-AG-UNDER-ILOCK). No write fails and no data is at risk. The path-fault rows ( docs/mpath-verification.md ) run under load on every node: one path lost and returned and then the other, a whole storage network lost on every node at once, a flapping path, a mount and an unmount on one path, a node killed while the survivors are on one path, a fenced node whose dead path comes back, every path lost, a node that withdraws, and a lock command the target applied whose answer never arrived. "Installed packages" means the release packages on two nodes of each of Proxmox VE 9, RHEL 9.8, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13; those rounds attach on one path, so mpath is claimed on Ubuntu 24.04 only. Not covered for mpath : a second target or storage controller, Fibre Channel or SAS, more than two paths, other multipath settings, and automatic failback to a preferred path group. Every host in a cluster needs the same version. 0.90.116: two-host Proxmox VE on DRBD: VM disks no longer freeze on slow SSDs, and a host that leaves, fails or rejoins comes back cleanly For 2/net/mesh/drbd , a VM's disk writes no longer freeze on slow disks. With seven AlmaLinux installs at once on two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts whose DRBD sat on 2011-era SATA SSDs, a guest write that needed new space could hold its disk image locked for 30 s to a minute. Its lock request had asked only to try, but it waited on the cluster's lock-ownership records, which were being written to the slow disk. Every other write to that image waited behind it, and the host kernel reported hung tasks. No write failed and no data was lost. 0.90.116's try never touches the disk and never waits: when its answer is not ready, it says so at once, the write takes space elsewhere, and a background worker readies the answer for next time. On the same disks and load, none of the slow waits remained, no task hung, and all seven installs finished ( CHANGELOG.md , 0.90.115 and 0.90.116). A host whose MeshXFS mount is shut down and then rejoins no longer hangs or stalls. When a host's heartbeat writes stop long enough, the other host declares its mount dead, recovers it, and the host's guard unmounts and remounts it with no restart. On two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts that rejoin had two faults when the rejoining host held the lower heartbeat slot: its mount could wait minutes for an admission that never came (fixed in 0.90.113); its first reads could take 69 to 95 s, because its peer's requests for the lock pages those reads needed were queued behind a stream of other hand-offs (fixed in 0.90.114). No data was lost in either. Both were found by forcing the dropout on purpose ( tests/pve_pair_failover.sh withdraw-p0 ), as happened for real on 2026-10-06 when a swapping host's heartbeat writes stalled. Everyday use did not reach either one. CHANGELOG.md has what was measured, 0.90.108 to 0.90.114. What 0.90.116 was validated on: The six shared-LUN configurations under "Released" below ( 2/net/mesh/direct , 4/net/mesh/direct , 2/disk/caw/direct , 4/disk/caw/direct , 8/disk/caw/direct , 16/disk/caw/direct ): the 31-row suite of each on the test rig (Ubuntu 24.04, iSCSI, one path per node) at its node count, and the installed packages on two nodes of each of Proxmox VE 9, RHEL 9.8, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13. 2/net/mesh/drbd : the DRBD rig ( tests/drbd_release_verify.sh ), the nested Proxmox VE 9 pair through every step of tests/pve_pair_failover.sh (crashes, power cuts, restarts, promotions, a slow heartbeat and the withdrawals), and the two physical Proxmox VE 9.1 hosts: seven concurrent AlmaLinux 9.7 installs at a time on MeshXFS on DRBD, on both the hosts' Samsung 850 EVO and their older Kingston SATA SSDs, and repeated dropout-and-rejoin laps under load. 8/net/mesh/direct , 16/net/mesh/direct and every mpath configuration were not tested on this release and are not claimed. 0.90.107: MeshXFS on DRBD dual-primary is released again, verified on two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts 2/net/mesh/drbd is released again : two hosts, each with its own local disk, replicated by DRBD dual-primary, with MeshXFS mounted read/write on both and no shared storage at all. It was withdrawn on 2026-10-06, after eight concurrent VM installs on two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts shut both hosts' MeshXFS mounts down and gave the guests I/O errors. What that load found was fixed ( CHANGELOG.md , 0.90.55 to 0.90.107), and this release was verified on those same two hosts as well as on the test rig: Two physical Proxmox VE 9.1 hosts (HP Z400, SATA SSDs, gigabit; kernel 6.17.2-1-pve, DRBD 8.4.11), installed with make install as docs/drbd-setup.md describes: seven AlmaLinux 9.7 installs at once, three on one host and four on the other, every guest disk on the shared filesystem, for 43 minutes. No guest I/O error, hung task, kernel warning, withdrawal or self-fence on either host. A nested Proxmox VE 9 pair , for the failures nobody should cause on hardware: a crash of either host, both hosts' power cut at once, a clean reboot, a host that dies while its peer is being repaired (four ways), stale and racing promotions, a slow heartbeat, and four withdrawals, each under a VM-like load on both hosts with every fsynced file checked on both afterwards. All 15 passed. The test rig (Ubuntu 24.04, DRBD 8.4.11, tests/drbd_release_verify.sh ): the cluster suite on /dev/drbd0 , unmount and remount, a node crash, a cut replication link, a split with no tie-break, a device stacked on DRBD, both nodes' power cut, and a pair-outage recovery whose owner dies. All passed. What it is not: fast under heavy writes on modest disks. Both disks write everything and every write waits for both, so a pair has one disk's write capacity. On the physical pair one AlmaLinux install on MeshXFS takes 1.4–1.9 times as long as on a local disk, and XFS on the same DRBD takes about three quarters of MeshXFS's time. Seven installs at once did not finish in 43 minutes, and under that load one heartbeat write took 8.6 s (the lease is 60 s). A lone sequential writer gets about three quarters of what XFS gets on the same DRBD: MeshXFS bounds its own writes in flight on DRBD so that its coordination writes are never starved. Size the VMs on a pair to its disks. Each of these is an open record in the defect queue. Also fixed, for every configuration: unmounting a filesystem that had been shut down could free the lock manager under a background log task and crash the node. The six direct configurations that no open defect blocks, and all four platforms, were verified again on this build. The eight mpath configurations and 8/net/mesh/direct and 16/net/mesh/direct are not claimed by this release, because defects found after 0.90.51 reach them; see "Released in an earlier version" below. 0.90.51: multipath, verified by taking paths away The mpath attachment is released at 2, 4, 8 and 16 nodes with both lock managers: {2,4,8,16}/net/mesh/mpath and {2,4,8,16}/disk/caw/mpath . Every node reaches the shared LUN through a dm-multipath map over two iSCSI paths, each path on its own NIC and its own storage network. Each of the eight configurations passed the 31-row suite the direct configurations pass, and then the path-fault rows of docs/mpath-verification.md , all under load on every node: one path lost and returned and then the other, a whole storage network lost on every node at once, a flapping path, a mount and an unmount on one path, a node killed while the survivors are on one path, a fenced node whose dead path comes back, every path lost, a node that withdraws, and on disk/caw a lock command the target applied whose answer never arrived. A row passes only with no failed operation on any node, no node lost that the row did not kill, every stall under the bound, and every acknowledged file read back by checksum from another node. Making those rows pass took changes to the filesystem, not only to the rig: a node now registers its fencing key on each path itself and follows its paths as they come and go, the lone survivor's fence works with one registration per path, a disk/caw lock swap whose answer was lost is recognised as landed, and several faults that are not specific to multipath were found and fixed on the way (a lock wait that lost its registration, a refused lock upgrade that starved behind its own node's readers, a healthy node shutting down behind a stalled peer, a survivor opening a dead node's files as directories, a lookup failing when its name was removed under it). CHANGELOG.md has each with what was measured. What this covers: iSCSI; two paths on separate networks to ONE target; the multipath and initiator settings in tools/mpath_settings.sh , which are the ones to use; the test rig's platform, Ubuntu 24.04 with kernel 6.8.0-101-generic and multipath-tools 0.9.4. What it does not: a second target or storage controller, Fibre Channel or SAS, more than two paths, other multipath settings, automatic failback to a preferred path group, and the other three platforms, whose package rounds attach on one path. The eight direct configurations and all four platforms were verified again on this build. 0.90.42: sixteen nodes 16/net/mesh/direct and 16/disk/caw/direct are released. Sixteen nodes mounting one LUN, with either lock manager, passed the same 31-row suite the smaller clusters pass — data integrity, coherency, crash and fence recovery, pace against native XFS — on the build this release ships, and the 2-, 4- and 8-node configurations and all four platforms were verified again on it. Two defect records stood between 8 nodes and 16. One was disproved by measurement. The other was a real fault in the disk/caw lock manager's clean-up after an abandoned lock wait, found by reading the code and never seen on the rig: the clean-up could act on a lock slot that had since been reused for a different lock. The check that stops it from releasing that other lock was already in the tree; this release adds a deterministic test for it and fixes what the test then showed — when the slot had been reused, the abandoned wait's own registration was left behind, which stalls every other node's readers of that lock. See CHANGELOG.md . 0.90.41: MeshXFS on DRBD dual-primary — a clustered filesystem with no shared storage Two nodes, a local disk each, no SAN, no iSCSI target, no third server. DRBD replicates the two disks synchronously (protocol C) with both nodes Primary at once, and MeshXFS mounts /dev/drbd0 read/write on both. The configuration is 2/net/mesh/drbd . This is the smallest possible MeshXFS cluster: two Proxmox hosts with local NVMe can share one filesystem for VM images and live migration without buying storage. DRBD has no SCSI underneath, so it has neither persistent reservations (how MeshXFS fences a dead node) nor COMPARE AND WRITE (how it claims heartbeat and recovery records). MeshXFS supplies both from the attachment itself: Fencing through an authority outside both nodes. DRBD's fencing resource-and-stonith freezes I/O when a node loses its peer and runs MeshXFS's handler, which has the site's fence authority (IPMI, a PDU, the hypervisor) power the peer off and hold it off. The authority grants one winner per split. The survivor proves the peer is off, disconnected and Outdated (fence proof kind 25) before every irreversible recovery step. Admission by a witness. A mount is refused unless DRBD is on protocol C with two primaries, MeshXFS's fence handler, every split-brain policy set to disconnect , no suspended I/O, and this node a working, UpToDate Primary. A compare-and-swap on the replicated device : a two-party one-bit lock in reserved sectors, with swaps group-committed under one acquisition. Recovery after both nodes lose power : the first node back has the authority hold its peer off, replays both journals, then lets the peer rejoin. Measured on the rig (two nodes, DRBD 8.4.11, Ubuntu 24.04, the 0.90.41 module built from the tree): the cluster suite's rows all passed, the fault rows and crash_audit included; a power cut of both nodes recovered with every file of both nodes intact, also when the recovery's completion was refused partway and finished by a resume; a recovery whose owner died was taken over and finished, by the owner's next boot and by the other node, every file intact; a node crash with a writer running was fenced, certified and recovered in 84 s with every fsynced file of both nodes intact; a link cut settled in 11 s and a split had exactly one winner in 11 s; unmount/remount cycles, a crash-cut retirement and a whole-cluster restart left nothing stalled; a device stacked on DRBD, and a loop device, were refused and left byte-identical. Cold chk_mxfs clean after each. Status: withdrawn on 2026-10-06 and released again in 0.90.107 (see the top of this file). 0.90.41 released it on Ubuntu 24.04 with DRBD 8.4.11, the platform and DRBD version everything above was measured on. Setup is in "DRBD dual-primary" under Quick start, the design in docs/attachment-methods.md ("DRBD dual-primary"), and the design rulings in docs/rulings/drbd-dual-primary-attachment.md . 0.90.41 is the first published DRBD release. The attachment was built in 0.90.40, whose release validation found three ways a second fault during pair-outage recovery could leave a volume unmountable; 0.90.40 was held back, all three were fixed, and the tests that found them are part of what passed above. A pair outage on 2/net/mesh/direct is also no longer left REFUSED when the other host is still booting. Also since 0.90.39, for every configuration: a stacked device is never resolved to the disk underneath it for SCSI passthrough, a compare-and-swap never falls back to a plain write, a node joining after a whole-cluster bootstrap settles the adopted victim's lock records (reads of the inodes they covered used to hang), and a departing node hands its lock pages off in parallel. See CHANGELOG.md . 0.90.39: mkfs.mxfs is no longer slow If you tried MeshXFS before and the format alone put you off, try it again. mkfs.mxfs used to take tens of seconds on a small LUN and minutes on a large one, where mkfs.xfs takes a moment. It now formats a 20 GB LUN in a quarter of a second. LUN before 0.90.39 10 GB 12.4 s 0.13 s 20 GB 17.9–30.9 s 0.24 s The cause was the lock authority ledger, which mkfs lays out on the LUN and sizes with it. mkfs wrote every empty page of it as its own synchronous 4 KiB write, about 2.3 ms each: 10,571 of them for 20 GB, 67,650 for 128 GiB, so the wait grew with the LUN. It now writes them in large batches, flushes once at the end instead of opening the device O_SYNC , and computes CRC32C in hardware. The formatted device is byte-for-byte identical: its sha256 matches the old binary's output at 10 GB and 20 GB. Every board of this release formatted its LUN with it, and the 8-node boards' cold audit read clean on every node. Also in 0.90.39: Fixes for races that could crash or wedge a node , all in the slots that let a lock-release drain re-enter the inode lock. A design review found three; this version's own self-test found a fourth. None was seen on the rig before the fixes. A release drain that cannot claim a slot is now queued and retried instead of run without one. 0.90.37 has these races, so upgrade from it. The RPM builds again. The 0.90.38 source tarball was missing a header the new mkfs needs. All six released configurations were verified on this version, and the release boards now run side by side, each on its own fixed-size test LUN. Shared SAN or DRBD storage · Network or on-disk locking · Fencing and journal recovery MeshXFS is an open-source (GPL-2.0) clustered filesystem. Built on XFS, it supports concurrent read-write mounts on shared iSCSI SAN storage—validated with 2, 4, 8, and 16 nodes—or on dual-primary DRBD, with network-based or SCSI COMPARE AND WRITE locking. MeshXFS provides fencing and survivor-led journal recovery, is packaged as a DKMS module for Proxmox VE 9, RHEL 9, Ubuntu 24.04, Ubuntu 26.04, Debian 12 and Debian 13, and includes a Proxmox VE storage plugin. On a system, MeshXFS goes by its short name mxfs : the mxfs.ko module, mount -t mxfs , the tools mkfs.mxfs , chk_mxfs ( fsck.mxfs ), resize_mxfs and mxfs_admin , and the mxfs and pve-storage-mxfs packages. A shared-LUN clustered filesystem written entirely by AI. Every line of the clustering, coordination, distributed-lock, fencing, and on-disk-envelope code in this repository was written by AI — not by a human using an AI tool. Claude Opus, running as an autonomous coding agent in Anthropic's Claude Code, wrote a large share of it, consulting Claude Fable, GPT, Gemini and Astra on the hardest problems. MeshXFS starts from the upstream Linux kernel XFS code, written by the XFS developers, and the AI has since modified much of it heavily (see "How this was built"). Everything that turns XFS into a filesystem many machines can mount at once is AI-authored. Every host in a cluster needs the same version. For 2/net/mesh/drbd , a VM's disk writes no longer freeze on slow disks. With seven AlmaLinux installs at once on two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts whose DRBD sat on 2011-era SATA SSDs, a guest write that needed new space could hold its disk image locked for 30 s to a minute. Its lock request had asked only to try, but it waited on the cluster's lock-ownership records, which were being written to the slow disk. Every other write to that image waited behind it, and the host kernel reported hung tasks. No write failed and no data was lost. 0.90.116's try never touches the disk and never waits: when its answer is not ready, it says so at once, the write takes space elsewhere, and a background worker readies the answer for next time. On the same disks and load, none of the slow waits remained, no task hung, and all seven installs finished ( CHANGELOG.md , 0.90.115 and 0.90.116). A host whose MeshXFS mount is shut down and then rejoins no longer hangs or stalls. When a host's heartbeat writes stop long enough, the other host declares its mount dead, recovers it, and the host's guard unmounts and remounts it with no restart. On two physical Proxmox VE 9 hosts that rejoin had two faults when the rejoining host held the lower heartbeat slot: No data was lost in either. If you tried MeshXFS before and the format alone put you off, try it again. mkfs.mxfs used to take tens of seconds on a small LUN and minutes on a large one, where mkfs.xfs takes a moment. It now formats a 20 GB LUN in a quarter of a second. The cause was the lock authority ledger, which mkfs lays out on the LUN and sizes with it. mkfs wrote every empty page of it as its own synchronous 4 KiB write, about 2.3 ms each: 10,571 of them for 20 GB, 67,650 for 128 GiB, so the wait grew with the LUN. It now writes them in large batches, flushes once at the end instead of opening the device O_SYNC , and computes CRC32C in hardware. The formatted device is byte-for-byte identical: its sha256 matches the old binary's output at 10 GB and 20 GB. Every board of this release formatted its LUN with it, and the 8-node boards' cold audit read clean on every node. All are fixed and verified since 0.90.37: The release bar: no open defect that can lose data, or crash, hang or shut down a node. A configuration has to clear it to be released, and tools/defects.py <configuration> --release shows it for each one. The defect queue itself is public ( data/defects.json , read with tools/defects.py ), and every record carries its evidence. It holds 123 open records. 54 of them reach only configurations this release does not claim, such as clusters larger than 16 nodes. The 69 that reach a released configuration (between 11 and 45 each, depending on the configuration) are each classified as not crossing that bar, most of them as slowness in a particular operation: tools/defects.py --at 2/net/mesh/drbd -d lists them for one configuration. Verified attachments on shared storage: direct and mpath , over iSCSI. With direct each node ran its own iSCSI initiator and reached the shared LUN on one path with nothing between MeshXFS and the target.
